newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Unemployment down in C.Europe except Czech - study.
newsitem.headline: Unemployment down in C.Europe except Czech - study.

text.p: Unemployment figures in Hungary, Poland and Slovakia suggest falling jobless rates but the Czech Republic will remain an exception, J.P. Morgan analysts said in a new report.

"Data suggest that the big jump in unemployment attending the early years of transition, up to the peaks recorded in 1994, are these days being - gradually - unwound in Hungary, Poland and Slovakia," they said in the weekly "Data Watch: Central Europe."
J.P. Morgan analysed unemployment figures in the four states and said the contrasting economic fortunes of the countries have shown up strikingly in their unemployment rates over the past 12 months.

"The divergence between Poland and the Czech Republic is especially noteworthy," they said. "In Poland, strong activity has steadily trimmed the jobless rate - to 11.6 percent this past June from over 14.3 percent one year earlier."

"In the Czech Republic, by contrast, slowing output growth along with declining corporate profitability has led to a persistent climb in the number of unemployed, albeit from low levels by regional standards," they said.
Czech jobless levels stayed around three percent throughout most of the period before heading upwards in recent months.

Developments in Hungary were less pronounced, with the jobless rate falling to 10.3 percent in June from 11.3 percent a year ago, as the output recovery has been modestly improving the jobless figures since the start of 1997, they said.
The analysts said that not only the levels of employment and unemployment changed but there have also been significant shifts in the structure of employment.

In industry, employment fell in all four countries from 1992 to 1996. In agriculture, employment also fell in all but Poland, where employment in the sector rose to 26.8 percent in 1996 from 25.8 percent in 1992.

In services, employment rose to 52.3 percent from 46.6 percent in the Czech Republic, to 59.1 percent from 53.6 percent in Hungary, to 55.5 percent from 48.9 percent in Slovakia, and edged up to 42.6 percent from 41.5 percent in Poland.

"This shift to employment in the tertiary sector is a clear manifestation of how the transition economies are coming to look increasingly like their western neighbours," J.P. Morgan's analysts concluded.
